title: Motion Engineering: Opus 5.5 哪里会翻车、怎么抓
html:
Opus 5.5 rendered my mascot in brand orange
Then I measured it
#E2A276
That is not orange. That is peach
9 of my 10 films missed the brand orange on the first measurement
In another film a coffee mug sat inside the character's body
On 373 of 420 frames
I had reviewed that film still by still
Not one review sheet showed it
Everyone is posting what Opus 5.5 can make
Almost nobody posts what it got wrong on the way
That is why the clips rhyme with each other. Same prompts, same defaults, same unnoticed mistakes
People call it brief contagion
The fix is not a longer prompt
It is knowing where the model is wrong, and which check catches it
I went through the review notes of ten films I have made with Opus 5.5
Three.js and Blender. Mascots, a Disney parody, a rocket launch, kinetic type, a 3D X feed
This is one of them:

Ten films, more than 100 logged defects
They are not random
They fall into a small number of classes, and every class has a check that catches it and a check that misses it completely
This is the ladder, level by level, with the real defect that opens each level, the block to paste into your brief, and the failure that pushes you to the next one


How these films are made, in 30 seconds
If you have never made a video with code, this is the whole pipeline:

Opus never touches pixels directly
That is the good news: every defect below lives in code, so every defect can be fixed with an edit and a re-render
It is also the bad news: Opus never sees the film unless you show it

The 30-second map
Every defect I logged belongs to one of these classes:


And the ladder you climb to catch them:



Level 0: One-shot
You write a prompt
Opus writes the code, renders, encodes
You watch the MP4 once, it looks good, you post it
Look at who checked what:

At 60 fps, a defect that lives for 69 frames lasts just over a second
You will not see it while you watch the film
You will see it the moment someone replies with a screenshot
What breaks: the film looks finished and is not. And everything Opus did not know, it filled in with its defaults

Level 1: Facts it may not invent
My first full render of a 3D X feed looked finished
The post text was grey bars
The brief said real post text. Opus drew placeholders, because placeholders look fine at a glance
The handle read @ m4lka instead of @m4lkxx. The avatar pointed at a stand-in image instead of the real file
In another film the Claude logo on a laptop was a drawn asterisk
It looked terrible. It took one line to fix: use the real spark from the reference folder
None of these are rendering problems
They are facts the model was allowed to make up

So split the brief in two:

And one rule above both:

A convincing fake interface is still a fake interface
What breaks: the facts are right, and the film still looks like everyone else's

Level 2: Rules, not references
Clawd Rave started from a reference video: a creature dancing in a gaming room, filmed by the webcam on the desk
The first render had a front camera, a plain red box room and wavy stripes on the monitor
Nothing was wrong with it
It was just the room every model builds
"Make it look like the reference" leaves Opus to decide what "like" means. It copies the most visible surface and misses the structure underneath
So convert every reference into numbers and roles:

Then check it the same way: the reference frame and your frame side by side, at the same timestamps
Once the reference was written as rules, the final came back as a different film

The final, every move on the kick:

What breaks: every element is right, and the shot is wrong. The face is behind the monitor. The title is off the frame

Level 3: States before effects
This is where most of my defects live
The wide shot is so far away the characters are 40 px tall and half the frame is empty floor
The monitor covers the face of the man who is the whole joke
The intern's monitor covers the other character's face in the sequel
The moon sits inside a glowing arc and reads as a second comet
The dragon flies straight across "The End"
A cream title sits on a cream moon
Here is the sequel after the states were written down. Every face clear, every beat readable:

None of this is about motion
It is about what the viewer should see at each moment, and nobody wrote it down
So write states, with timestamps, before any scene code:

Each beat names the thing that must be visible, so a still can prove it
And treat frame 1 as its own beat
My Disney parody opened from black with a fade in
On X, the first frame is the thumbnail. The feed autoplays it without sound
A black first frame is a black thumbnail
It now starts on the lit castle

Same lesson in another film: twelve effects popped in one by one, so the opening frames showed only part of the grid. Now all twelve are live from frame 0

What breaks: you want to check a beat at 13.7 s, so you render 13.7, and the frame does not match the film

Level 4: Any frame on demand
The contract everyone writes is one line:

Then the libraries break it without telling you
A text scramble froze: the same glyphs frame after frame, the original text showing through. The plugin keeps its own internal time between calls, so every frame depends on the one before it
A physics wall of bricks was already scattered on frame 0. The engine wakes every sleeping body on its first step
A laptop screen drifted out of frame during a hold. The smooth keyframe curves overshot the pose it was meant to hold
One effect reset the transparency and broke the fade of every layer drawn after it
Each of these looks fine in the live preview
Each of them gives you a still that lies

The last line is the test. If two renders of the same frame differ, nothing you measure later means anything
What breaks: the frames are honest now, and there are 1,080 of them. You are not going to watch them all

Level 5: The contact sheet
A full MP4 is the most expensive way to find out that a title clips on frame 148
Render stills at every beat, plus three frames 1/60 s apart around every transition, and put them on one sheet
My rocket film had 12 defects on the first sheet
Six on the second
Five on the third, then the final render
That is what a converging loop looks like on paper
The rocket film after round four:

The sheet is where the model's blindness to 3D shows up most clearly:

Opus writes the number. It does not see where the number points

The sheet catches the renderer's own physics too:
Dark slashes inside the word "Clawd". It sat on the same plane as a transparent "Disney", and the ray skipped one face

A huge red streak the frame before every crack. Hidden objects were parked at the origin, and motion blur smeared them across the frame
That one is from this film. Watch the cracks: there is no streak now

Snow that was invisible with a correct material, and rain eaten by the denoiser, because each streak was under a pixel wide
A 6 px flame lost to the denoiser. A white flash that blanked two whole frames
Then hand the sheet back with a narrow question:

"It feels off" is a mood. A frame number and a cause is a task
What breaks: the sheet looked clean for three rounds, and the mug was inside the body the whole time

Level 6: Instruments
Here is the defect that changed how I review
Remember the film at the top of this article? The character holds a coffee mug and sips from it
Every review sheet looked fine
Then I watched the film and saw the mug sinking into the body
A script that tests mesh points against the torso box, every frame, found it on 373 of 420 frames. The cup was 4.9 cm inside the body on the sip
Same story in the Disney film. A cookie inside the torso on 69 frames, two characters inside each other during the hug on 47 more
The sheet samples 20 frames. Contact lives between them

Color is the same. Nine films out of ten missed the brand orange on the first probe:

"Make it more orange" is a mood
#E2A276 → #D97757 is a target, and you know when you have hit it

And then there is the file you ship, which is not your source:
A vignette filter in backward mode brightened the edges instead of darkening them. Dark films hid it. The first bright meadow showed white corners
It happened in two different films
The default audio encoder pushed one crack past the clipping point
The audio stream came out 12.011 s against 12.000 s of video
The instruments I now run on every film:

The model does not get to grade its own work. The judge is the render, the reference or a measurement
What breaks: everything measurable passes. And the film is still wrong in a way no script knows how to ask about

Level 7: The loop learns
Three defects in my notes no instrument would ever catch:
The black first frame
The "Tesla" that read as a random sedan
The Claude logo that just looked bad
Taste. That one is yours
So put yourself where only a person can see, and nowhere else:

Then make every defect pay once
The two-faces-on-one-plane bug hit me twice. Letters in one film, snow in another
The backward vignette hit me twice
Both times it was the same lesson, learned from scratch
A lesson only sticks when it lands on the layer that owns it:

"Be careful with transparent planes" in a prompt is a hope
An offset rule in your house file, plus a check that fails, is structure
The test for this level is simple:
The same class of defect never costs you twice

Who catches what
The table I wish I had before film one:


The model can review the sheet. It cannot review between the frames, and it cannot review taste

Which level are you on?


Find your first symptom from the top
That is your next level. Not the one after it

The checks, ready to paste

The last line matters most. My best review notes all end with it

The short version
Opus 5.5 is good enough that the first render looks finished
That is exactly the problem
Facts stop it from inventing
Rules stop it from defaulting
States make the point visible
Seeking makes every frame honest
The sheet makes defects cheap
Instruments see between the frames
And you guard the one thing nothing else can: whether it is any good

Every film in this article has its prompt pack as a PDF: the brief, the beats, the checks. Drop one into Opus 5.5 and see what it makes
All of them are free in my Telegram: t.me/m4lka4
If this was useful, bookmark it for the day your mascot comes out peach
Follow @m4lkxx for more on how agent systems actually work
Longer breakdowns on my Substack: https://substack.com/@m4lkxx
My projects on GitHub: https://github.com/m4lka
And the same Telegram has shorter notes, new tools and the setups I am testing
